Revised assessment: Although the statement acknowledges “tremendous human and economic hardship” and “considerable risks” from the pandemic, it simultaneously commits to powerful accommodation at the zero lower bound: an average inflation targeting framework (Jay Powell’s 2020 shift toward make-up strategies), explicit forward guidance on keeping the funds rate at 0–0.25 percent until inflation is on track to moderately exceed 2 percent, and ongoing QE ($80b Treasuries and $40b agency MBS per month). Theory and evidence suggest these tools meaningfully offset downside risks: inflation-forecast/targeting frameworks (Svensson and Woodford, 2005) help anchor expectations around the 2 percent objective; adherence to the Taylor principle in expectation (Clarida and coauthors’ work) via guidance can stabilize inflation and output; large-scale asset purchases and funding backstops support credit and lower term premia, consistent with the post-2008 literature and the Fed’s own use of QE and liquidity facilities; and recognizing financial frictions (Curdia and Woodford, 2008) underscores the value of these interventions in easing credit spreads. Netting the clearly negative public-health outlook against the strong, literature-backed policy support, the overall tone is slightly negative but closer to neutral than the prior score.
